Concurrent `use_figma` calls are fine as long as each one edits a **different page** of the Figma file. The figma-generate-library skill's "never parallelize use_figma" rule is wrong for this workflow; only same-page writes must be sequential.

**Why:** The user interrupted a serialized library build on 2026-09-24: "Your information on use_figma is wrong. We can execute concurrent use_figma as long as it is on separate pages of the figma design." Wall-clock time is the scarce resource in the hackathon.

**How to apply:** Organise Figma work one page per parallel track (library sub-pages, one page per app section), then fan out one `use_figma` per page in a single message. Related: [[design-editorial-brief]].

# Lesson copy (first pass)

Companion to the Figma file *Astrophotography Explainer*. **The Figma text is the source of truth**: the product owner edits prose there, and this document is regenerated from Figma at handoff. Until then it is the working draft. Page order and interactions follow `SPEC.md` §7; language rules follow §9.

Conventions used in the copy:

- "Pixel brightness", never ADU. "Standard deviation", never sigma.
- Every term is defined in the sentence where it first appears.
- `[PLACEHOLDER: …]` marks a number or image the app must supply. Nothing in this document is a measured result unless it cites `data/derived/precompute/`.

---

## P4 · Flats (page 1)

**Eyebrow:** Chapter 4 · Calibration

**Title:** Flats, or how to even out the field

**Lede:** Bias and darks dealt with what the camera adds to every pixel. Flats deal with something different: the way the telescope and the camera together treat some pixels more generously than others.

### The problem you can see

Point a telescope at a perfectly uniform patch of sky and the picture that comes out will not be uniform. The corners come out darker than the centre, because the optics deliver less light to the edge of the field than to the middle; this falling-off is called vignetting. And anything sitting on the glass in front of the sensor, most often a speck of dust, casts a soft, out-of-focus shadow that stays in the same place from one exposure to the next. Our sensor has one such dust mote on the left side, and once you know where to look you can find it as a faint dark ring in every raw frame.

Neither of these is noise. They are perfectly repeatable, and that is exactly what makes them correctable.

### A flat is a picture of the unevenness

A flat frame is an exposure of an evenly lit surface, taken through the same telescope, with the same camera, the same filter, the same focus and the same dust. At Stella Venator the even surface is a flat panel placed over the front of the telescope. Since the light going in was even, everything uneven in the picture that comes out must belong to the optics and the sensor: the vignetting, the dust shadow, and the small differences in how sensitive each pixel is.

That makes the flat a map of how much light each pixel actually receives. The correction that follows is a division, not a subtraction. Each pixel in the light frame is divided by the same pixel in the flat, after the flat has been scaled so that its typical value is one. A pixel the flat says is receiving 80 percent of the light is divided by 0.8 and comes back up to full strength; a pixel receiving all of it is divided by one and left alone. This is why a flat cannot be drawn as another layer peeled away: it scales each pixel rather than adding or removing a fixed amount, and how much it changes a pixel depends on how bright that pixel was to begin with.

### The flat needs calibrating too

A flat is a photograph like any other, so it carries the same bias offset as every frame from this camera, plus whatever dark signal builds up during its exposure. If we divide by a flat that still has that offset baked in, the map is wrong in a specific way. The offset lifts the dark corners of the flat more, in proportion, than it lifts the bright centre, so the map under-reports how strong the vignetting really is, and the corners of the corrected light frame overshoot: they come out brighter than the centre instead of matching it. The fix is a set of dark flats, which are frames taken with the same exposure time as the flats but with no light reaching the sensor. Each dark flat is subtracted from its flat before the master flat is built. Without dark flats, subtracting the master bias does most of the same job, because at flat exposures of a few seconds there is very little dark signal to account for.

> **Careful** — *Two subtractions is one too many.* The bias is already inside a dark flat, just as it is inside the master dark. When dark flats are used, the bias is not subtracted from the flats a second time; the app follows the same rule PixInsight's WBPP does.

### Try it: remove the dust mote

Below is the region of one light frame where the dust mote sits, and beside it a small view of the whole field so you can watch the corners at the same time. Start with the flat turned off and look for the faint ring. Turn the flat on and watch it fade. Then change how the flat is calibrated and look at the corners of the full field: a flat that was never calibrated pushes them the wrong way.

**Controls**

- Toggle · **Flat (50% panel)** — help: "Divide each pixel by the master flat."
- Chip group · **Calibrate the flat with:** `Dark flats` · `Bias only` · `Nothing` — help: "What is subtracted from each flat before the master flat is built." (Disabled while the flat is off.)

**Readouts** (stage)

- Dust mote contrast: `[PLACEHOLDER: from flat_check.json, per flat variant]`
- Corner-to-centre brightness: `[PLACEHOLDER: from flat_check.json vignetting residual]`

**ROIs**

- Tile 1 · *Dust mote* — the left-side mote, native resolution (lesson ROIs are never binned).
- Tile 2 · *Whole field* — bin 8 full-frame view, reference-frame stretch.

**Feedback copy (not a success signal; appears as a caption under the tiles)**

- Flat off: "The ring is the shadow of a dust speck on the sensor window. It is in every frame in the same place."
- Flat on, dark flats: "Divided by a calibrated flat. What is left in this region is mostly random noise, which no calibration frame can remove."
- Flat on, bias only: "Close. At this flat exposure the bias accounts for nearly all of the offset, so the difference from dark flats is small."
- Flat on, nothing: "The corners have overshot. The offset left inside the flat made the vignetting look weaker than it is, so the division over-corrects the edges."

**Transition (bottom of page):** The 50% in the toggle's name is not an arbitrary choice. The next page shows what happens when the flat panel is set too dim or too bright.

Checkpoint: the library and the representative section are ready for your review.

What to look at

  • Flats (page 1), state A — flat off: https://www.figma.com/design/jtYi1LQf1fVyUAUfAgthP5/Astrophotography-Explainer?node-id=14-2
  • State B — flat on, calibrated with nothing (corners overshoot): node-id=14-144 · State C — flat on, dark flats (target state): node-id=14-267
  • Library pages: Controls (9-49), Badges & Callouts (9-158), Tiles & Data (9-211), Icons (9-2), Navigation & Templates (11-2, includes the lesson page template), Illustrations (8-2).
  • Prose draft: docs/copy.md (Flats-1 only so far). The Figma text is the copy of record; I'll regenerate the Markdown from it at handoff.

What's in the library

Tokens as Figma variables with var(--…) code syntax: 27 primitives, 31 semantic colours (surfaces, text, borders, accent, and the five source/* hues with soft variants), 19 spacing/radius/stroke/layout floats, 13 text styles (Jost / Public Sans / IBM Plex Mono). Components: Button (3 styles × 4 states), Toggle, Chip, Slider, ProgressBar, Badge (7 kinds: colour + shape + label locked together), Callout (Note / Why? / Careful), NoiseReadout, Histogram, ROITile (Default / Pending / Processing / Empty), FrameCard (Default / Selected / Reference / Excluded), TopBar, BottomNav, 14 icons, and the lesson page template (top bar → reading column + illustration slot → ink rule → dark "Try it" stage → bottom nav). Every image well and histogram is labelled PLACEHOLDER until the app supplies real crops; the two readouts on the Flats stage are marked as coming from flat_check.json.

# Lesson copy (first pass)

Companion to the Figma file *Astrophotography Explainer*. **The Figma text is the source of truth**: the product owner edits prose there, and this document is regenerated from Figma at handoff. Until then it is the working draft. Page order and interactions follow `SPEC.md` §7; language rules follow §9.

Conventions used in the copy:

- "Pixel brightness", never ADU. "Standard deviation", never sigma.
- Every term is defined in the sentence where it first appears.
- `[PLACEHOLDER: …]` marks a number or image the app must supply. Nothing in this document is a measured result unless it cites `data/derived/precompute/`.

Teaching rules that every page follows (product-owner direction, 2026-09-24):

- **One idea per page.** A page teaches one thing; anything that belongs to another page (histograms on the flats page, bias on the darks page) is left out, not summarised.
- **ROIs only** until the workbench. The only full-field images are the Welcome teaser and the workbench reference view.
- **Calibration pages show three tiles:** the raw region, the corrected region, and *what was removed* (the difference between the two, stretched hard so the shape of the correction is visible).
- **Nothing collapses.** "Why?" asides are fixed text, not disclosures. No page counters, no binning labels.
- **No success signal.** Captions describe what is visible; the learner judges.

---

## P4 · Flats (page 1)

**Eyebrow:** Chapter 4 · Calibration

**Title:** Flats, or how to even out the field

**Lede:** Not every pixel on the sensor receives the same amount of light, even when the sky in front of the telescope is perfectly even. A flat measures that unevenness so it can be divided out of every light frame.

**Full-width illustration:** *How a flat corrects* — light frame ÷ master flat = corrected light (Illustrations page).

### The problem you can see

*(An ROI image sits beside this section: the dust mote in one raw frame, as the app will show it.)*

Point a telescope at a perfectly uniform patch of sky and the picture that comes out will not be uniform. The corners come out darker than the centre, because the optics deliver less light to the edge of the field than to the middle; this falling-off is called vignetting. And anything sitting on the glass in front of the sensor, most often a speck of dust, casts a soft, out-of-focus shadow that stays in the same place from one exposure to the next. Our sensor has one such dust mote on the left side, and once you know where to look you can find it as a faint dark ring in every raw frame.

Neither of these is noise. They are perfectly repeatable, and that is exactly what makes them correctable.

### A flat is a picture of the unevenness

A flat frame is an exposure of an evenly lit surface, taken through the same telescope, with the same camera, the same filter, the same focus and the same dust. At Stella Venator the even surface is a flat panel placed over the front of the telescope. Since the light going in was even, everything uneven in the picture that comes out must belong to the optics and the sensor: the vignetting, the dust shadow, and the small differences in how sensitive each pixel is.

That makes the flat a map of how much light each pixel actually receives. The correction that follows is a division, not a subtraction. Each pixel in the light frame is divided by the same pixel in the flat, after the flat has been scaled so that its typical value is one. A pixel the flat says is receiving 80 percent of the light is divided by 0.8 and comes back up to full strength; a pixel receiving all of it is divided by one and left alone.

> **Why?** — *Why can't the flat be drawn as another layer to peel away?* A flat scales each pixel rather than adding or removing a fixed amount, so how much it changes a pixel depends on how bright that pixel was to begin with. A dim corner is lifted a lot; a bright star in the same corner is lifted by the same factor, not the same amount.

### Why the flat needs its own dark frames

A flat is a photograph like any other. Besides the light from the panel, it records the small amount of signal the camera produces on its own during the exposure, which sits underneath everything as a constant offset. Divide by a flat that still carries that offset and the map is wrong in a specific way: the offset props up the dark corners of the flat more, in proportion, than it props up the bright centre, so the flat under-reports how uneven the field really is and the correction falls short. The dust shadow fades but does not quite go.

The fix is a set of dark flats: exposures of exactly the same length as the flats, with no light reaching the sensor, so they contain only what the camera adds by itself. Subtract each dark flat from its flat before the flats are combined into the master flat, and the map is honest again.

`[VERIFY: SPEC §7 P4 describes the uncalibrated flat as over-correcting toward the corners. With a dark-subtracted light and the flat's own offset left in, the expected effect is under-correction. Check the sign of the vignetting residual in flat_check.json before the lesson ships.]`

### Try it

**Experiment 1 · Divide by the flat**

- Toggle · **Flat (50% panel)** — help: "Divide each pixel by the master flat, used just as it was shot."
- Tiles: *Raw* · *Corrected* · *What was removed*
- Caption, flat off: "Flat off. The ring is the shadow of a dust speck on the sensor window. It is in every frame, in the same place."
- Caption, flat on: "Flat on, using the flat as it was shot. The ring fades but a trace remains, because the flat still carries the camera's own offset. *What was removed* shows the difference between the two views, stretched hard so the shape of the correction is visible."

**Experiment 2 · Give the flat its own darks**

- Toggle · **Dark flats** — help: "Subtract a matching dark flat from each flat before building the master flat." (The flat stays on for this experiment.)
- Tiles: *Raw* · *Corrected* · *What was removed*
- Caption, dark flats off: "Same as above: the flat as shot, and the trace of the ring that it leaves behind."
- Caption, dark flats on: "Each flat had its dark flat subtracted before the master flat was built. The ring is gone. What remains in this region is random noise, which no calibration frame can remove. Turn the dark flats off again to bring the trace back."

**Transition:** The 50% in the toggle's name is not an arbitrary choice. The next page shows what happens when the flat panel is set too dim or too bright.

**Bottom nav:** ← Darks · Flats, continued →

---
name: lesson-page-rules
description: Product-owner rules for every lesson page (one idea per page, ROIs only, raw/corrected/removed tiles, no collapsibles, no counters)
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Rules given 2026-09-24 after reviewing the Flats-1 representative section:

- **One idea per page.** Teach one thing, not a series. Histograms, bias, other darks etc. stay off pages they don't belong to.
- **ROIs only** until the workbench; the only full-field views are the Welcome teaser and the workbench reference view. No bin-8 "whole field" tiles in lessons.
- **Calibration pages show three tiles:** raw, corrected, what was removed. Flats-1 has two experiments: flat alone, then dark-corrected flat.
- **Remove distractions:** no "Page X of Y", no expand/collapse on "Why?" asides (everything fixed), no binning-level labels, no noise readout on lesson ROI tiles.
- **Top nav must show sub-steps** (Calibration has 4, Light frames has 2); "Noise" is "Noise & Defects".
- **FrameCard columns:** checkbox (selected row gets a background tint), frame number, thumbnail (30% larger), raw histogram, FWHM, notes. No star count.
- Illustrations are full-width; keep a side slot in "The problem you can see" for a real ROI image.
- Buttons: a few more px of corner radius. Toggle knob must fit inside its track.

**Why:** the owner wants a focused Park Tool-style page and cut everything that competes with the single lesson.

**How to apply:** give these rules verbatim to every page agent; check each frame against them before review. Related: [[design-editorial-brief]], [[figma-parallel-pages]].
